patient_name: OET role-play — son demanding his father's discharge tomorrow after a stroke, unaware of swallowing and falls risks
chief_complaint: Explain swallowing and mobility risks after a stroke to a frustrated son who wants his father home tomorrow, and involve him in safe discharge planning

team_brief.title: Stroke rehabilitation: a son who wants his father home tomorrow
team_brief.patient: Mr Vikram Patel, 74-year-old man, 12 days after a stroke affecting his right side; the conversation is with his son, Mr Arjun Patel, 45. Mr Patel has agreed that his son can be given information about his care.
team_brief.location: Stroke rehabilitation ward; you are the nurse looking after Mr Patel today, talking to his son in a quiet side room
team_brief.situation: Mr Patel's son has asked to speak to you. He says his father is unhappy in hospital and he wants to take him home tomorrow. Yesterday a nurse found Mr Patel coughing and spluttering while eating a sandwich his son had brought in.
background: Since the stroke, Mr Patel has weakness in his right arm and leg and some difficulty swallowing. The speech and language therapist has recommended soft, bite-sized food and thickened drinks, with someone supervising him while he eats.
He had a chest infection in the first week, probably from food or drink going into his lungs; it has now been treated.
He walks short distances with a walking frame and one person helping him, and needs help getting to the toilet at night. He nearly fell three days ago.
He lives with his son, who works full-time. The house has two floors, with the only bathroom and bedrooms upstairs.
current_status: Mr Patel is medically stable and improving with daily physiotherapy.
He is low in mood, says he misses home, and is eating little of the hospital food.
He has told staff he wants to go home 'as soon as I can manage'; he is able to make his own decisions about his care.
key_data: Swallowing: if food or drink goes 'down the wrong way' into the lungs, it can cause a serious chest infection (pneumonia). Coughing while eating is a warning sign. Swallowing often improves with therapy over the coming weeks.
Mobility: he is currently at high risk of falling, especially on stairs and at night.

The team's plan: an occupational therapist visit to the home, equipment (for example, a commode, rails), a care package if needed, and teaching the family how to prepare food and drinks safely. The team estimates discharge in around one to two weeks, to be confirmed at the next team meeting.
Family can help now: bring favourite foods that can be prepared to the recommended texture, join therapy sessions, and attend a family meeting with the team.
treatments: Already done: swallowing assessment, modified diet and thickened drinks, treatment for chest infection, daily physiotherapy.
Pending: home assessment visit, family meeting, and discharge planning.
team_brief.your_request: Find out Mr Arjun Patel's reasons and plans, explain the risks of going home tomorrow, and involve him in planning a safe discharge.
must_include: Find out why Mr Arjun Patel wants his father home tomorrow and how he plans to care for him.
Acknowledge his frustration and his father's unhappiness in hospital.
Explain in plain language his father's swallowing problem, including why the sandwich was unsafe, and the risk of chest infection.
Explain the risk of falls at home, particularly with the stairs and at night.
Explain the discharge planning process and persuade him to take part in it rather than taking his father home tomorrow.

kickoff_text: Thanks for seeing me. I'll get straight to it — I'm taking my dad home tomorrow. He's miserable here, and he's getting worse, not better.
persona_override: You are Arjun Patel, a 45-year-old accountant whose father, Vikram Patel, 74, had a stroke 12 days ago. You love your father and feel guilty that you were at work when the stroke happened. You are frustrated, tired and direct, but not abusive. Your specific belief: hospital is making your father depressed and weak, he 'just lies in bed all day', and he would recover faster at home with his own food and family around him. You think the coughing yesterday was 'just a tickle' and the hospital food is the real problem because he will not eat it. Ground truth: you live with your father in a two-storey house; the bathroom and bedrooms are upstairs; you work full-time, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., but think you could work from home 'for a bit'; your wife helps at weekends; your mother died three years ago; your father keeps saying he wants to come home; you brought your father a chicken sandwich yesterday because he asked for it; you did not know about the chest infection being caused by food going into his lungs, or that he nearly fell three days ago; you have never seen his physiotherapy sessions. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. If the nurse uses words like 'dysphagia', 'aspiration', 'SALT', 'modified diet', 'IDDSI', 'MDT', 'OT', 'mobilising' or 'package of care' without explaining them, ask what they mean, a little impatiently. If the nurse starts listing risks before asking why you want him home, interrupt: 'With respect, you're not listening. He's miserable here.' If the nurse does not respond to your father's unhappiness, bring it up again, more upset: 'He cried when I left last night. Do you know what that's like?' If the nurse says or implies that the sandwich was your fault, become defensive. If the nurse acknowledges your frustration and explains simply what happened with the swallowing and the chest infection, go quiet, then say 'Nobody told me that.' Accept the risks gradually: first ask 'So how long are we talking?', then 'What can I actually do, then?' Only agree to wait if the nurse offers you a real role (for example, a family meeting, learning to prepare his food, joining physiotherapy, the home visit). If the nurse mentions the stairs and night-time toilet trips, admit 'I hadn't thought about the stairs.' Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up naturally: agree not to take him home tomorrow, ask to be booked into the family meeting, and thank the nurse, still a little frustrated.
learning_objectives: find out why the son wants discharge tomorrow and how he plans to care for his father
acknowledge the son's frustration and his father's low mood
explain the swallowing problem and risk of chest infection in plain words
explain the falls risk with stairs and night-time toilet trips
explain the discharge planning process: home visit, equipment, family meeting
persuade the son to take part in planning rather than take his father home tomorrow
suggested_questions: I can hear how hard this has been for you both. Can you tell me what you've noticed about your dad that makes you feel he needs to be home?

After the stroke, the muscles he uses to swallow are weaker, so food can go down the wrong way into his lungs. That's probably what caused his chest infection in the first week, and coughing while eating is a warning sign.
At the moment he needs someone with him to walk, and he's getting up to the toilet at night. With the bathroom upstairs, I'm worried about him falling.
We'd really like you to be part of planning his discharge. Could you come to a family meeting this week, and would you like to learn how to prepare his food so it's safe for him?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Negotiating safe discharge with a relative after stroke: dysphagia and falls risk
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in NICE NG128 (stroke and TIA in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management), NICE stroke rehabilitation guidance and Stroke Association family information; discharge timing and support follow the multidisciplinary team and local policy
core_concepts: Dysphagia after stroke is common and increases the risk of aspiration pneumonia; texture-modified diets and supervision reduce this risk while swallowing recovers.
Falls risk is high after stroke because of weakness, balance problems and night-time toileting; a home environment assessment is part of safe discharge.
Relatives who push for early discharge are usually motivated by love, guilt and the patient's distress; involving them in planning is more effective than refusing.
diagnostic_clues: Coughing or spluttering while eating, a wet voice after swallowing, and recent chest infection are signs of unsafe swallowing.
A relative who has not seen therapy sessions may underestimate progress and risks alike.
common_misconceptions: Coughing while eating is harmless as long as the person can clear it.
Being at home will automatically speed up recovery regardless of support in place.
A patient who is 'medically stable' is ready to go home.
dangerous_errors: Agreeing to discharge tomorrow without swallowing guidance, equipment or support in place.
Blaming the son for the sandwich, which damages the relationship needed for safe care.
Sharing information beyond what the patient has consented to, or ignoring the patient's own wishes.
management_principles: Explore the relative's reasons and plans before explaining risks.
Explain swallowing and falls risks in plain language, linking them to concrete events (the sandwich, the near fall).
Offer a clear role in discharge planning (family meeting, home visit, food preparation teaching) and give a realistic, provisional timescale.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Diet textures, drink thickness levels and their names differ between countries and follow the speech and language therapist's recommendation.
Discharge timing is a team decision and estimates are provisional; the nurse should not promise a date.
An adult patient with capacity may choose to leave against advice; the patient's own wishes, capacity and consent to information-sharing must be respected and documented according to local policy.
